Comeliness
KUM-lee-ness
noun
From the Saxon cymlic, becoming or seemly, related to become — that which is fitting, graceful, and proper to its object. Comeliness is not mere prettiness but propriety: the beauty of a thing being what it ought to be.

Biblical Definition

Comeliness is fitting beauty, and Scripture’s uses of it converge on a single startling place. Ezekiel tells Jerusalem that her renown went forth among the heathen for her beauty, “for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee” (Eze 16:14) — a borrowed loveliness, lent and not owned. Daniel, seeing the great vision, reports that “my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength” (Dan 10:8); the sight of glory undoes a man’s own dignity. And then Isaiah, of the Servant: “he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isa 53:2). The One who put comeliness upon Jerusalem had none Himself. That is the exchange the chapter goes on to describe in every other particular — He bore our griefs, He was wounded for our transgressions, the chastisement of our peace was upon Him — and the beauty is part of the transaction. Paul completes the doctrine at the level of the body: “those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness” (1Co 12:23). God’s way with beauty is to put it where men would not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Fitting or becoming beauty; grace and propriety rather than mere attractiveness. Bestowed by God on His people, absent from His Servant, and given by Him to the parts men count least.

COMELINESS, n. That which is becoming, fit, or suitable; grace; beauty; dignity.

From comely; Saxon cymlic, becoming, seemly, allied to become.

Distinguished from beauty: comeliness is propriety and fitness rather than mere form.

Applied to conduct as well as appearance; that which is seemly in a person’s station.

Isa 53:2: he hath no form nor comeliness, said of the suffering Servant.

Key Scripture

Isa 53:2 — "For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him."

Eze 16:14 — "And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD."

Dan 10:8 — "Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength."

1Co 12:23 — "And those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness."

Modern Corruption

Appearance has become a currency by which people are ranked and valued, which is exactly the scale Isa 53:2 refuses — the Redeemer had nothing on it.

expand to see more

The corruption is the tyranny of appearance. Every age has valued beauty; ours has industrialised it, measuring, ranking, and rewarding it at a scale no previous generation could manage, and training people from childhood to regard their own faces as assets to be optimised. The gospel strikes at this from an unexpected direction. It does not chiefly say that inner beauty matters more, true as that is. It says that when God came to save, He came without any of it: no form nor comeliness, no beauty that we should desire him. The most important Person who ever lived would not have been ranked at all, and if the scale cannot register Him the scale is worthless.

Recover the plain sense: comeliness in Scripture is bestowed, not possessed. Jerusalem’s was my comeliness, which I had put upon thee — loveliness on loan, which she then prostituted. Daniel’s own comeliness turned to corruption the moment he saw real glory, which is what happens to every human excellence brought near the throne. And Paul’s rule for the body settles how the church should behave: the parts we think less honourable receive more abundant honour, and the uncomely parts more abundant comeliness — God deliberately compensating where men would discount. A congregation ordered on that principle looks nothing like the world’s ranking, and is meant not to.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon cymlic, becoming — fitting beauty; lent to Jerusalem, absent from the Servant, given to the parts men count least.

expand to see more

Comeliness — Saxon cymlic, seemly, becoming; allied to become.

Propriety and fitness rather than mere attractiveness of form.

Eze 16:14: my comeliness, which I had put upon thee — beauty on loan.

Dan 10:8: a man’s comeliness turns to corruption before true glory.

Isa 53:2: the Servant had no form nor comeliness at all.

Usage

"If the scale of appearance cannot register Christ, the scale is worthless."

"All human comeliness in Scripture is bestowed, and is undone before glory."

"1Co 12:23: God gives more abundant comeliness where men give least honour."
